title: Your circle

segments.voice: Yesterday, your mosque. Your line: belong somewhere. Did you greet someone by name and ask them a real question? A mosque on Friday is a crowd. Today, something smaller that can grow inside it. Day one thousand four hundred five.

A Tuesday evening. A living room with the couch pushed back. A pot of tea going cold because everyone forgot it. A handful of people on cushions in a rough ring, one mushaf open to a single page, and a question nobody can quite answer: what does this verse actually ask of us on a weekday? Someone checks a commentary. Someone else admits she always misread that line. A teenager asks the question the adults were too shy to ask. No microphone, no stage, no front row. Just a ring of knees. Today, a small study circle. The halaqah.
screen: `A RING OF CUSHIONS AND COLD TEA.` → `ONE PAGE, ONE QUESTION.` → `NO STAGE, NO FRONT ROW.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Halaqah means a circle, and it is what Muslims call a group that sits together to learn. Next, the promise attached to it. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that whenever people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting His Book and studying it among themselves, calm comes down on them, mercy covers them, angels surround them, and Allah mentions them to those who are with Him. Notice what the hadith describes. Not one person reading alone. People studying among themselves. Third, why a circle and not a lecture. In a circle everyone faces the middle. The quiet person can be seen. A question can come from anywhere. The Qur'an, in surah al-Ma'idah, says in Pickthall's words: "Help ye one another unto righteousness and pious duty." A circle is a very practical way to help one another: you keep each other coming back, and you hear the parts of a verse you would have skimmed. Last, what keeps a circle honest. A circle can drift into everyone sharing opinions with nothing underneath them. So a circle does well to keep one anchor: a teacher who visits, a trusted commentary, a book worked through page by page. And they keep a good habit of manners: one person speaks at a time, nobody mocks a question, and anyone may say, I don't know. Saying I don't know, out loud, in front of friends, is part of learning together.
screen: `HALAQAH: A CIRCLE TO LEARN.` · `CALM, MERCY, AND ANGELS AROUND.` · `EVERYONE FACES THE MIDDLE.` · `AN ANCHOR, AND I DON'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: The practice: join or start one. First, sit. Let your breath settle and your hands rest. In your mind, draw a small ring and seat a few people in it, people you would actually like to learn with: a friend, a cousin, a neighbor, someone from work. Don't pick the most impressive ones. Pick the ones who would show up. Now place one thing in the middle of the ring: a short surah, a single hadith, a chapter of a book. Notice how it feels to imagine not learning alone. If you pray, you can ask Allah, in your own words, to bless whatever circle you join. After the bell, send one message: either ask to join a circle, or invite two people to start one. The bell holds the time.
Halaqah. A circle of people who sit facing one another to learn their faith together. Today's word.
Your line: learn together. Today, share one thing you learned this week with one person, and ask what they make of it. Tomorrow, your charity. Day one thousand four hundred five.

howItsDone: Muslims gather in a halaqah, a study circle, at a mosque or in a home, to read a passage of the Qur'an or a hadith together, often with a teacher or a trusted commentary, and to discuss what it asks of daily life.

what a scholar hears: the hadith in Sahih Muslim promising calm, mercy, angels and Allah's mention to those who study His Book among themselves.
